The **Connection settings** card for the provider.
The **Mailbox signature** card. It appears for e-mail channels only.
**Cancel** and **Save changes**.
The **Status** card with **Test connection** and, for mailboxes, **Poll now**.
The **Danger zone** card with **Delete channel**.

blocks.tip: Select **Simulate** at the top right to open the simulator with this channel already chosen.

sections.title: Test a channel and fetch mail now
sections.intro: Test a channel after you create it or change its credentials. For a mailbox, you can also fetch new mail without waiting.
steps: Open the channel. See [Change a channel](#ch-change-channel).

steps.text: In the **Status** card, select **Test connection**.
steps.note: You can also select **Test** on the channel's card in the list.

steps.text: Read the result under the buttons.
steps.note: **Connected** means the test worked. **Failed** shows the reason.

steps: For a mailbox, select **Poll now** to fetch new mail at once.
sections.result: After **Poll now**, the panel shows how many e-mails were fetched, processed, skipped as duplicates and failed.

sections.title: Connect a channel to its provider
intro: WhatsApp, Messenger, Instagram, SMS and voice providers send messages to SupportDesk as they happen. They send them to a callback address that SupportDesk creates for each channel.
You enter this address at the provider once.
steps: Create and save the channel first.

steps.text: In the **Webhook** card, select **Copy URL**.
steps.caption: The status panel of a phone line with its callback address in the **Webhook** card.
steps.alt: Side panel with the Status card, the Webhook card with Copy URL and Rotate key, and the Danger zone

steps: Paste the address in the webhook setup at your provider.
For Meta, also enter the same **Webhook verify token** that you saved on the channel.
Send a test message from your phone to check that a ticket appears.
sections.result: New messages arrive in SupportDesk within seconds.
blocks: If the address leaks, select **Rotate key**. SupportDesk creates a new address.

blocks.warning: The old address stops working at once. Enter the new address at the provider right after you rotate the key.

blocks.note: SupportDesk builds the address from the web address in your browser. If you work on an internal address, replace it with your public address before you give it to the provider.

sections.title: Delete or deactivate a channel
sections.intro: Remove a channel you no longer use. SupportDesk keeps the history of channels that have conversations.
steps: Open the channel.
In the **Danger zone** card, select **Delete channel**.
In the confirmation, select **Delete**.
sections.result: A channel without messages is deleted, and the app shows **Channel deleted**. A channel with messages is switched off instead, and the app shows **Channel deactivated**.

blocks.tip: To pause a channel for a while, turn off **Active** and select **Save changes**.

sections.title: Set up the chat widget
sections.intro: The chat widget adds a chat button to your website. Visitors chat with the AI assistant or an agent without leaving your page.
prerequisites: You have a **Live chat** channel. To add one, follow [Add a channel](#ch-add-channel) and choose the **Live chat** type.
Someone can edit the pages of your website.
steps: Open the **Live chat** channel.

steps.text: In the **Widget** card, set the greeting, the switches and the offline message.
steps.caption: The **Widget** card of the website chat channel.
steps.alt: Widget card with Greeting, Bot answers first, Ask for e-mail before chatting, Offer e-mail verification, Offline message and Widget title

steps: Select **Save changes**.

steps.text: In the **Embed the widget** card, select **Copy embed code**.
steps.caption: The **Embed the widget** card with the code, **Live preview** and a preview of the chat window.
steps.alt: Embed the widget card showing the script code, Copy embed code, Live preview and a small preview of the chat window

steps: Give the code to your web team. They paste it before the end of the page body on each page.
To try the widget, select **Live preview**. A demo page opens in a new tab.
sections.result: The chat button appears on your website. New chats arrive in **Inbox** > **Live chat**.

sections.title: Chat widget options
sections.intro: These settings are in the **Widget** card of a **Live chat** channel.

rows: The first message visitors see when they open the chat.
The AI assistant replies first. It hands the chat to an agent when needed.
Visitors must enter their e-mail address before they can chat.
Visitors can confirm their e-mail with a one-time code. The chat then links to their contact.
Shown when no agent is available.
The title at the top of the chat window, such as `Chat with us`.

blocks: Your web team can add options to the embed code. They can fill in the visitor's name and e-mail. They can also open the chat at once or show the button on the left.

blocks.note: Agents take chats only if their **Max concurrent chats** is above zero. You set it on the agent's page in **Teams & Agents**.

sections.title: Acknowledgements and unknown senders
sections.intro: Two switches on a channel decide how SupportDesk treats new senders.
blocks: An acknowledgement is a short e-mail that confirms a new ticket. SupportDesk sends it only when both of these are on:

list: **Send automatic acknowledgements** on the mailbox.
The setting **Acknowledge new e-mail tickets automatically (where the mailbox allows it)** in ticket configuration.

blocks: Each sender gets at most three acknowledgements an hour. This stops e-mail loops with other automatic replies.
You can change the wording in the **New ticket acknowledgement** e-mail template. See the chapter on notification settings and e-mail templates.
When **Accept messages from unknown senders** is off, SupportDesk accepts messages only from known contacts. New e-mail threads and messages from other senders are refused.

sections.title: The channel simulator
intro: The channel simulator lets you test channels without real customers. It feeds messages, e-mails and call events into SupportDesk the same way real providers do.
The simulated messages create real tickets in your workspace. Use a test workspace, or close the test tickets afterwards.
blocks: To open it, select **Simulator** on the **Channels** page. You can also select **Simulate** on a channel.

blocks.caption: The simulator with a mailbox chosen and a sample e-mail filled in.
blocks.alt: Channel simulator form with numbered highlights on the Channel list, the form heading, the Deliver e-mail button and the Results card

callouts: **Channel** lists every active channel. The form below changes with the channel type.
The heading shows the address that receives the simulated traffic.
**Deliver e-mail** sends the e-mail into SupportDesk.
**Results** lists what happened to each simulated item, with links to the ticket and the inbox.

rows: The message was added to an existing ticket.
The message was already received, so it was skipped.
The message was not accepted, for example from an unknown sender.
A delivery receipt updated a sent message.
The simulation failed. The reason is shown in red.

blocks.note: Live chat is not simulated here. Open the demo page from the simulator and chat as a visitor. Then answer from **Live chat** in the inbox.

sections.title: Simulate an inbound e-mail
sections.intro: Send a test e-mail into a mailbox channel to see how SupportDesk creates or threads the ticket.
steps: Open the simulator and choose a mailbox in **Channel**.
Enter the **From address** and, if you like, the **From name**.
Enter the **Subject** and the **Body (plain text)**.

steps.text: To add the e-mail to an existing conversation, enter its Message-ID in **In-Reply-To**.
steps.note: To test duplicate handling, reuse a **Message-ID**. Otherwise leave it empty.

steps: Optionally choose an **Attachment** under 5 MB.
Select **Deliver e-mail**.
sections.result: A new line appears in **Results**. Select **Ticket** or **Open in inbox** to see the result.

sections.title: Simulate a WhatsApp, SMS or social message
sections.intro: Send a test message into a WhatsApp, SMS, Messenger or Instagram channel.

steps.text: Open the simulator and choose the channel in **Channel**.
steps.caption: The message form for a WhatsApp channel.
steps.alt: Simulator form for WhatsApp with Sender number, Sender name, Text, Provider message id, Media and Deliver message

steps: Enter the **Sender number**. For Messenger and Instagram, enter the **Sender id (PSID)**.
Enter the **Sender name** and the **Text**.
Optionally choose a **Media** file under 5 MB.
Select **Deliver message**.
sections.result: The message creates a ticket or joins the sender's open conversation. The outcome appears in **Results**.

blocks.tip: To test duplicate handling, reuse a **Provider message id**.

sections.title: Simulate a phone call
sections.intro: Send call events into a voice channel. A call is a series of events with the same **Call id**.

steps.text: Open the simulator and choose the voice channel in **Channel**.
steps.caption: The call event form for a phone line.
steps.alt: Simulator form for a voice channel with Event, Call id, Caller number, Direction, Agent e-mail, Duration, Recording URL, Notes and Send call event

steps: In **Event**, choose **Started (ringing)**.
Enter the **Caller number** and choose the **Direction**.
Select **Send call event**.
Keep the same **Call id**. Choose the next event, such as **Answered** or **Missed**, and send it.
For **Answered** and **Ended**, enter the **Agent e-mail** and the **Duration (seconds)**.
For **Voicemail**, enter the **Recording URL**.
To start another call, select **New call**.
sections.result: Missed calls and voicemails create tickets. Answered calls create tickets when the channel allows it.

sections.title: Check outbound messages and delivery receipts
sections.intro: The **Outbound messages** card lists what SupportDesk sent through the chosen channel, newest first.
steps: Open the simulator and choose a channel.

steps.text: Look at the **Outbound messages** card on the right. Select **Refresh** to update it.
steps.caption: Sent WhatsApp replies, with buttons to simulate a delivery receipt.
steps.alt: Outbound messages card with two messages, their status, attempts and Simulate receipt buttons Delivered, Read and Failed

steps: To test what agents see, select **Delivered**, **Read** or **Failed** next to **Simulate receipt**.
sections.result: The message status changes. Agents see the same status on the reply in the ticket.

chapters.title: Automation, blueprints and webhooks
intro: This chapter is for administrators. It explains rules, which automate routine work, and blueprints, which guide tickets through fixed steps. It also covers webhooks, which send events to other systems.
Every rule and blueprint has versions. You can test a change before it goes live, and you can go back to an earlier version.

sections.title: The Automation page
intro: To open automation, select **Automation** in the rail. You can also select **Administration** > **Automation & blueprints**.
You need the **Manage automation rules and blueprints** permission. The **Webhooks** tab appears only if you may also manage integrations.

blocks.caption: The **Rules** tab. Rules are grouped by the event that starts them.
blocks.alt: Automation page on the Rules tab with numbered highlights on the tabs, the search box, the trigger list, New rule, the first rule, its counts, its switch and its arrows

callouts: The tabs: **Rules**, **Executions**, **Blueprints** and **Webhooks**.
**Search rules** finds rules by name or description.
The trigger list shows the rules of one trigger only.
**New rule** opens the rule designer.
The rule's name, its description and its badges.
How many times the rule ran, and when it last ran.
The switch turns the rule on or off. You can switch on a rule only after you publish it.
The arrows move the rule earlier or later within its trigger.

rows: Version 1 is live. Only the published version runs.
The rule has never been published, so it never runs.
Someone saved changes that are not live yet.
Later rules on the same trigger do not run when this rule matches.
This rule may fight with another active rule. Point to the badge to read why.
A scheduled rule and how often it runs.

sections.title: How rules work
intro: A rule has three parts. **When** is the trigger, the event that starts the rule. **If** holds the conditions the ticket must meet. **Then** lists the actions that run, in order.
For example: when a ticket is created, and it is High priority from a VIP customer, raise it to Critical. Then notify a supervisor.
blocks: Rules with the same trigger run in the order shown on the **Rules** tab. A rule with **Stop processing later rules when this rule matches** ends the run for that event when it matches.
Each save creates a new version. Only the published version runs. You can test a draft first, then publish it.

list: Each event runs each rule version only once.
A rule never reacts to changes made by its own actions.
Chains of rules that start other rules stop after five steps.
One rule runs at most 20 times an hour on the same ticket.
A scheduled run handles at most 500 tickets.

blocks.note: Rules cannot delete tickets, merge them or mark them as spam. Agents do those things by hand.

sections.title: The rule designer
sections.intro: Select a rule's name, or select **New rule**, to open the rule designer.

blocks.caption: The rule designer with an existing rule open.
blocks.alt: Rule designer with numbered highlights on the toolbar, the name card, the When card and the side panel

callouts: The toolbar. It shows the live version and the **Active** switch. It also has **Change note (optional)**, **Check**, **Save draft** and **Publish**.
**Rule name**, **Description** and the stop-processing switch.
The **When** card, followed by the **If** and **Then** cards further down.
The side panel with the **Simulate**, **Versions** and **Conflicts** tabs.

blocks: At the bottom of a saved rule, **Delete rule** removes it.

sections.title: Create a rule
sections.intro: Create a rule to make SupportDesk act on tickets for you.
prerequisites: You have the **Manage automation rules and blueprints** permission.
steps: Select **Automation** > **Rules**, then select **New rule**.
Enter a **Rule name** and, if you like, a **Description**.
In the **When** card, select the trigger. See [Rule triggers](#au-triggers).
In the **If** card, add the conditions. See [Rule conditions](#au-conditions).
In the **Then** card, select **Add action** and choose an action. Fill in its fields.
Add more actions if you need them. Use the arrows to change their order.
If later rules must not run when this one matches, turn on **Stop processing later rules when this rule matches**.
Optionally enter a **Change note (optional)** that says what you changed.
Select **Save draft**.
sections.result: The app shows **Draft v1 saved**. The draft does not run yet. Test it, then publish it. See [Simulate a rule](#au-simulate-rule) and [Check and publish a rule](#au-publish-rule).

sections.title: Rule triggers
sections.intro: The trigger is the event that starts a rule. You choose one trigger per rule in the **When** card.

rows: A ticket is created from any channel.
Ticket fields change. In **Only when these fields change**, you can name the fields to watch.
The ticket's status changes. Use the **changed to** and **changed from** checks on the status.
The assignee or the team changes.
An agent sends a public reply.
The customer replies through any channel.
An internal or handover note is added.
An SLA target reaches its warning point.
Something happens on a customer account. The rule runs on the related or open tickets.
A set time passes. The rule checks open tickets every 5 minutes to 7 days.
Another system calls the rule's own web address with a ticket number.

sections.title: Rule conditions
intro: Conditions decide which tickets the rule acts on. A rule without conditions acts on every ticket for its trigger.
Each condition has a field, a check and a value. Select **Condition** to add one, or **Group** to add a group of conditions.

blocks.caption: Conditions for high-priority tickets from VIP contacts or Platinum customers.
blocks.alt: If card with two conditions joined by All (AND) and a nested group joined by Any (OR)

list: **All (AND)** means every condition in the group must be true.
**Any (OR)** means one true condition in the group is enough.
Groups can sit inside groups, up to four levels deep.
Select the bin icon to remove a condition. Select **Remove group** to remove a group.

rows: Exact values, such as a priority, status, team or customer.
**contains**, **does not contain**, **contains any of**, **starts with**, **ends with**
Words in text fields and tags.
A text pattern. Ask a technical colleague to write it.
Fields that are blank or filled in.
Time since a date, such as the last activity. Use them in scheduled rules.
What the triggering event changed, such as the status.

sections.title: Rule actions
intro: Actions run in the order listed in the **Then** card. Changes appear in the ticket history as **Automation:** followed by the rule name.
Text fields accept placeholders, such as `{{ticket.number}}` or `{{contact.name}}`. Select a placeholder chip under the field to insert it.

blocks.caption: The **Notify agents** action with its fields and the placeholder chips.
blocks.alt: Notify agents action with Recipients, Specific agents, Roles, Title and Message fields, placeholder chips and Severity

rows: Assigns an agent or team, or runs automatic routing again.
Moves the ticket to another department.
Escalates the ticket and notifies supervisors. It can also raise the priority.
Changes the priority or severity. SLA targets follow the new priority.
Changes the status. It is not allowed on blueprint tickets.
Fills in or clears a custom field.
Adds a note that only agents see.
Sends a reply template to the customer.
Adds agents as watchers, collaborators or specialists.
Creates a task or a linked child ticket.
Sends an in-app notification to chosen people.
Sends a message to the contact, the assignee or an address.
Calls another system's web address. Failed calls are retried.
Updates the related record in Wings ERP.
Asks a person or a role to approve something.
Lets the AI suggest a classification or write a summary.

sections.title: Run a rule on a schedule
sections.intro: A scheduled rule checks open tickets at a set interval. Use it for reminders and time limits, such as closing tickets that wait too long.
steps: Open the rule designer.

steps.text: In the **When** card, select **Scheduled**.
steps.caption: The **Scheduled** trigger with the **Run every (minutes)** field.
steps.alt: When card with the Scheduled trigger selected and Run every (minutes) set to 60

steps: In **Run every (minutes)**, enter a number from 5 to 10080.
In the **If** card, add a time condition, such as **older than (minutes)** on the last activity.
Add the actions, then select **Save draft**.
sections.result: After you publish and activate the rule, the list shows how often it runs. The designer shows the next run time.

blocks.warning: A scheduled rule without conditions acts on every open ticket on every run. **Check** warns you about this.

sections.title: Let another system start a rule
sections.intro: With the **Inbound webhook** trigger, another system can start a rule for a ticket. For example, your ERP can add a note when a payment arrives.
steps: Open the rule designer and select **Inbound webhook** in the **When** card.
Add the conditions and actions, then select **Save draft**.
Copy the **Webhook URL** that now appears in the **When** card.

steps.text: Copy the secret in the yellow box and select **Copy**.
steps.warning: The secret is shown only once. If you lose it, select **New secret** and give the new one to the other system.

steps: Give the address and the secret to the person who sets up the other system.
sections.result: The other system can now start the rule. Each call names a ticket by its number.
blocks: Values that the other system sends can be used in conditions and texts. In the **If** card, enter a field name and select **Add payload field**. In texts, use the placeholder `{{webhook.<field>}}`.

sections.title: Simulate a rule
sections.intro: A simulation shows what a rule would do to real tickets. It changes nothing on the tickets.
steps: Open the rule and select the **Simulate** tab in the side panel.
Choose **One ticket** and enter a **Ticket number**. Or choose **Most recent** and enter the **Number of tickets**, up to 50.
To test your unsaved edits, turn on **Use the unsaved changes in the editor**.

steps.text: Select **Run simulation**.
steps.caption: The **Simulate** tab before a run.
steps.alt: Simulate tab with One ticket and Most recent options, Number of tickets and Run simulation

sections.result: The panel shows how many tickets matched. Each ticket shows **Matches** or **No match**, the check of every condition, and each action as **would run** or **skipped**.

blocks.note: Simulations appear on the **Executions** tab with the status **Simulated**.

sections.title: Check and publish a rule
sections.intro: Publish a rule to make it live. Only the published version runs.
steps: Open the rule and select **Check**.
If a red box lists problems under **Fix these before publishing:**, fix each one.
Read any yellow warnings, such as a scheduled rule without conditions.
Select **Publish**.
Turn on the **Active** switch in the toolbar.
sections.result: The app shows **Published v1** (or the next version number). The toolbar shows **Live: v1**.

blocks.tip: To switch a rule off quickly, turn off its switch on the **Rules** tab. The app shows **Rule deactivated**.

sections.title: Compare and roll back rule versions
sections.intro: Every save of a rule is a version. Use the **Versions** tab to see what changed and to go back.

steps.text: Open the rule and select the **Versions** tab.
steps.caption: The **Versions** tab with the published version 1.
steps.alt: Versions tab showing v1 with the Published and in editor badges, its date, author, change note, Open and Diff

steps: To see what changed, select **Diff** on a version. Added lines start with + and removed lines start with -.
To load an old version into the editor, select **Open**.
To make a draft live, select **Publish** on it.
To return to an older published version, select **Roll back** on it and confirm.
sections.result: A rollback publishes the old definition again as a new version. The old version stays in the history.

sections.title: Rule conflicts
sections.intro: SupportDesk compares active rules that share a trigger. It flags rules that may undo each other's work.

list: Two rules set the same field to different values.
Two rules assign the same tickets to different people or teams.
One rule adds a tag that another rule removes.
A rule stops processing before another rule can run.

blocks: The **Rules** tab shows the number of conflicts. In the designer, the **Conflicts** tab explains each one and links to the other rule.

blocks.tip: Most conflicts go away when you change the order of the rules or add a condition.

sections.title: Change the order of rules
sections.intro: Rules with the same trigger run from top to bottom.
steps: Select **Automation** > **Rules**.
Clear **Search rules**. You cannot reorder while a search is active.
Drag a rule by its grip, or select the up and down arrows next to it.
sections.result: The new order applies to the next event.

sections.title: Delete a rule
sections.intro: Delete a rule you no longer need. To keep it for later, switch it off instead.
steps: Open the rule.
At the bottom, select **Delete rule**.
In the confirmation, select **Delete**.
sections.result: The app shows **Rule deleted**. The rule and its versions are gone. Its execution history stays.

sections.title: Review rule executions
sections.intro: The **Executions** tab records every time a rule was checked. It shows what matched, what each action did and why rules were skipped.

blocks.caption: The **Executions** tab with the newest runs first.
blocks.alt: Executions tab with numbered highlights on the rule, status and trigger lists, the ticket box, Apply, a status badge and Details

callouts: Show the runs of one rule.
Show the runs with one status.
Show the runs of one trigger.
Enter a ticket number to see the runs on that ticket.
**Apply** filters the list. **Clear** removes the filters.
The status of the run.
**Details** opens the condition check and the result of each action.

rows: The conditions matched and every action worked.
Some actions worked and some failed.
The run was stopped to prevent an endless chain of rules.
The ticket did not meet the conditions. Nothing happened.
A test run from the **Simulate** tab. Nothing changed.

blocks.note: The **Depth** column shows how many rules ran before this one in the same chain.

sections.title: See why a rule ran and retry failed actions
sections.intro: Open a run to see each condition and each action. You can run failed actions again.
steps: Select **Automation** > **Executions**.
Filter the list if needed, then select **Apply**.

steps.text: Select **Details** on a run.
steps.caption: The **Execution details** panel for a scheduled rule that closed a ticket.
steps.alt: Execution details panel with the status, rule, trigger, ticket, times, the conditions table and two succeeded actions

steps: Read the **Conditions** table. A green tick means the condition was true.
Read the **Actions** list. Failed actions show the reason in red.
If the run failed, select **Retry failed actions**.
sections.result: The app shows **Retried** and the new status of the run.

sections.title: How blueprints work
intro: A blueprint guides tickets through fixed states, such as investigation, fix, release and closed. Each step can need fields, a comment or an approval.
Blueprints need the blueprints feature of your plan.

list: A blueprint applies to new tickets of a department, a category, or both. If several blueprints fit, the most specific one wins.
A state sets the ticket's status and substatus. One state is the starting state, and some are final states.
A transition moves the ticket from one state to another. It can check roles, ask for fields and comments, or need an approval.
Agents run transitions from the ticket's **Blueprint** tab. They cannot change the status of a blueprint ticket directly.

blocks: Administrators with the automation permission can still change the status directly. They can also select **Remove ticket from blueprint** on the ticket.

blocks.caption: The **Blueprints** tab with one published blueprint.
blocks.alt: Blueprints tab with numbered highlights on the ticket box with Open ticket blueprint, New blueprint, the blueprint name with its switch, its badges and its footer

callouts: Enter a ticket number and select **Open ticket blueprint** to see that ticket's progress.
**New blueprint** opens the blueprint designer.
The blueprint name and its **Active** switch.
The department, the category and the published version.
How many open tickets follow the blueprint, and when it was last changed.

sections.title: The blueprint designer
sections.intro: Select a blueprint's name, or select **New blueprint**, to open the designer. You draw the states and transitions on a canvas.

blocks.caption: The **Defect escalation** blueprint in the designer.
blocks.alt: Blueprint designer with numbered highlights on the toolbar, the settings card, the canvas tools, the canvas and the inspector

callouts: The toolbar with **Active**, **Check**, **Save draft** and **Publish**.
**Blueprint name**, **Department**, **Category** and **Description**.
The canvas tools: **Add state**, **Connect from selected** and **Delete selected**.
The canvas. Each box is a state, and each arrow is a transition.
The side panel with the **Inspector** and **Versions** tabs.

list: Drag a state to move it. When a state has focus, the arrow keys move it.
Drag the arrow handle of a state onto another state to add a transition.
Select a state or a transition to edit it in the **Inspector**.

sections.title: Design a blueprint
sections.intro: Create a blueprint to make tickets follow a fixed process.
prerequisites: You have the **Manage automation rules and blueprints** permission.
The statuses and substatuses you need already exist in ticket configuration.
steps: Select **Automation** > **Blueprints**, then select **New blueprint**.
Enter the **Blueprint name**. Choose the **Department**, the **Category**, or both.
Select **Add state** for each step of the process, then fill in each state in the **Inspector**.
Turn on **Initial state (new tickets start here)** for the first state, and **Final state** for the last ones.
Select a state, select **Connect from selected**, then select the target state.
Select each transition and fill in its fields in the **Inspector**.
Select **Check** and fix any problems it lists.
Select **Save draft**, then select **Publish**.
Turn on the **Active** switch.
sections.result: The app shows **Published v1**. New tickets that match the department or category follow the blueprint.

sections.title: Blueprint state fields
sections.intro: Select a state on the canvas to see these fields.

blocks.caption: The **Investigation** state in the **Inspector**.
blocks.alt: Inspector showing the State fields Name, Key, Ticket status in this state, Substatus, the Initial state and Final state switches and the transitions from here

rows: The state name agents see on the ticket.
A short fixed id in lower case. Other systems use it.
The status the ticket gets in this state. Empty keeps the current status.
The substatus the ticket gets, if the status has substatuses.
New tickets start in this state.
The process ends in this state.
Starts a new arrow from this state.
Removes the state and its transitions from the draft.
Links to the arrows that leave this state.

sections.title: Blueprint transition fields
sections.intro: Select an arrow or its label on the canvas to see these fields.

blocks.caption: The **Confirm defect** transition with roles, mandatory fields and an approver.
blocks.alt: Inspector showing the transition fields Name, Key, From, To, Allowed roles, Mandatory fields, Comment required, Approval, Validation and After the transition

rows: The button label agents see, such as `Confirm defect`.
A short fixed id for the transition.
The states where the transition is offered. Choose several, or leave it empty for any state.
The state the ticket moves to.
Who may run the transition. Empty means anyone who can edit the ticket.
Fields the agent must fill in, such as severity, product or root cause.
The agent must write a comment.
**No approval**, **A specific person**, **Anyone with a role** or **Department supervisors**.
Who approves, for the person and role choices.
A short note shown with the approval request.
Conditions the ticket must meet. Values entered with the transition count.
The message agents see when the validation fails.
Actions that run after the move, chosen with **Add action**.
Removes the arrow from the draft.

blocks.note: With **Department supervisors**, anyone who may decide approvals can approve the request.

sections.title: Turn off, version or delete a blueprint
sections.intro: Blueprints have the same versions as rules.
steps: To stop a blueprint for new tickets, turn off its switch on the **Blueprints** tab.
To see older versions, open the blueprint and select the **Versions** tab.
On a version, select **Open** to load it, **Diff** to compare it, or **Publish** to make a draft live.
To delete a blueprint, open it without selecting anything on the canvas. Select **Delete blueprint** in the **Inspector** and confirm.
sections.result: The app confirms each change with a message.

blocks.note: **Delete blueprint** is greyed out while open tickets follow the blueprint. Close or move those tickets first.

sections.title: How webhooks work
intro: A webhook sends a message to another system each time something happens in SupportDesk. Examples are a new ticket, a customer change or a published article.
Every message is signed with a secret. The receiving system uses the signature to check that the message came from SupportDesk.
blocks: To open webhooks, select **Administration** > **Webhooks**, or the **Webhooks** tab on the **Automation** page. You need the permission to manage integrations.

blocks.caption: The **Webhooks** page with one disabled example webhook.
blocks.alt: Webhooks page with numbered highlights on New webhook, the webhook details, its last delivery, its switch, Deliveries and the more actions menu

callouts: **New webhook** adds a webhook.
The name, status, address and events of the webhook.
When the last message was delivered, and the answer code.
The switch enables or disables the webhook.
**Deliveries** opens the delivery log.
The menu with **Edit**, **Send test ping**, **Rotate secret** and **Delete**.

rows: Recent deliveries failed. A red badge shows how many failed in a row.
Nothing is sent. You or SupportDesk switched the webhook off.

list: A failed delivery is retried, first after 30 seconds and finally after 12 hours.
After 8 attempts, the delivery stops with the status **Dead letter**.
After 20 failures in a row, SupportDesk disables the webhook and notifies administrators.
Webhooks cannot call addresses inside your own network unless your server administrator allows it.

sections.title: Add a webhook
sections.intro: Add a webhook to send SupportDesk events to your ERP, chat tool or data warehouse.
prerequisites: You may manage integrations.
You have the web address of the receiving system.
steps: Select **Administration** > **Webhooks**, then select **New webhook**.
Enter a **Name**.
Enter the **Payload URL**, the full web address of the receiving system.
Under **Events**, tick the events to send. Or tick **All events (current and future)**.

steps.text: Optionally enter a **Signing secret** of at least 16 characters.
steps.note: If you leave it empty, SupportDesk creates one for you.

steps.text: Leave **Enabled** on and select **Create webhook**.
steps.caption: The **New webhook** panel with a name and an address filled in.
steps.alt: New webhook panel with Name, Payload URL, the Events list, Signing secret, Enabled and Create webhook

steps.text: Copy the signing secret from the yellow box and select **Copy**.
steps.warning: The secret is shown only once. Give it to the receiving system before you select **Dismiss**.

sections.result: The app shows **Webhook created**. Select **Send test ping** in the webhook's menu to test it.

sections.title: Edit, test or delete a webhook
sections.intro: Use the webhook's menu for changes and tests.

steps.text: Select the menu button at the end of the webhook's row.
steps.caption: The webhook menu.
steps.alt: Menu with Edit, Send test ping, Rotate secret and Delete

steps: Choose **Edit** to change the name, address, events or secret. Then select **Save**.
Choose **Send test ping** to send a test message now. The app shows **Ping delivered** or **Ping failed**.
Choose **Rotate secret** to create a new secret, then confirm. Copy the new secret from the yellow box.
Choose **Delete** and confirm to remove the webhook and its delivery log.
sections.result: The list shows the changed webhook.

blocks.warning: After **Rotate secret**, the receiving system rejects messages until it has the new secret.

sections.title: Check deliveries and redeliver
sections.intro: The delivery log shows every message sent by a webhook, with the answer from the receiving system.
steps: On the webhook's row, select **Deliveries**.
To filter the log, choose a status, such as **Failed (retrying)** or **Dead letter**.

steps.text: Select a delivery to open it.
steps.caption: The delivery log of a webhook that has not sent anything yet.
steps.alt: Deliveries panel with the status list, Refresh, Send test ping and the list of deliveries

steps: Read the attempts, the times, the **Response** and the **Payload**.
To send it again, select **Redeliver**.
sections.result: The app shows **Queued for redelivery**. Select **Refresh** to see the new attempt.

blocks.note: **Redeliver** is greyed out while the webhook is disabled. Fix the receiving system, turn the webhook on, then redeliver.

chapters.title: AI and knowledge settings
intro: This chapter is for administrators. It explains how to set up the AI that helps agents and customers, and how to control its cost.
It also shows where the knowledge base settings are, because the AI answers from your knowledge base.

sections.title: The AI settings page
intro: To open it, select **Administration** > **AI**. You need the **Manage AI models, prompts, budgets and agents** permission. AI also needs the AI feature of your plan.
The header shows whether AI is on and which provider it uses. **AI Assistant** opens the agents' AI workspace.

blocks.caption: The **Provider & budget** tab of the **AI settings** page.
blocks.alt: AI settings page with numbered highlights on the tabs, the Model provider card, the Embeddings and knowledge index card, the Budget and cost card, the Privacy and retention card and Save settings

callouts: The tabs: **Provider & budget**, **Features**, **Auto-reply scenarios**, **Prompt templates**, **AI agents**, **Usage & cost** and **Execution log**.
**Model provider**: the AI service, the **AI enabled** switch and **Test saved provider**.
**Embeddings & knowledge index**: how SupportDesk searches by meaning, and **Reindex knowledge now**.
**Budget & cost**: the monthly limit and what happens when it is used up.
**Privacy & retention**: personal data protection and how long the log is kept.
**Save settings** saves the whole tab. It is greyed out until you change something.

blocks.note: Every AI call passes the same checks. SupportDesk checks permissions and the budget, hides personal data and records the call in the log.

sections.title: AI providers
sections.intro: The provider is the AI service that writes summaries, drafts and answers. You choose one provider for the whole workspace.

rows: Built in, offline and free. Nothing leaves your servers. It cannot translate.
Your own OpenAI resource in Microsoft Azure.
Any service that works like OpenAI, such as a model your company hosts.
The Anthropic service. It cannot search by meaning, so keep **Local** for embeddings.

blocks: The key is stored encrypted and is never shown again. To delete a saved key, tick **Remove the stored key**.

sections.title: Choose the AI provider
sections.intro: Switch from the built-in provider to an external AI service, or back.
prerequisites: For an external provider, you have its model name and key from your AI account.
steps: Select **Administration** > **AI**. The **Provider & budget** tab opens.
Make sure **AI enabled** is on.

steps.text: Choose the provider.
steps.caption: **OpenAI** chosen, with the fields for that provider below.
steps.alt: Model provider card with OpenAI selected, the Model field filled in, an empty Endpoint field and the key field

steps: Enter the **Model**, or the **Deployment name** for Azure OpenAI.
Enter the **Endpoint** if your provider needs one. The hint under the field tells you.
Paste the key into **API key**.
Select **Save settings**.
Select **Test saved provider**.
sections.result: The test shows **Chat OK** with the response time, and **Embeddings OK**. If a part fails, the reason appears under the badges.

blocks.note: The test uses the saved settings. Save your changes before you test.

blocks.tip: To switch AI off for everyone, turn off **AI enabled** and select **Save settings**.

sections.title: Set the AI budget
sections.intro: External AI services charge for each use. Set a monthly budget so that the cost cannot run away. The built-in provider is free.
steps: On the **Provider & budget** tab, find the **Budget & cost** card.
Enter the **Monthly budget**. Enter `0` for no limit.
Enter the **Currency**, such as `USD` or `INR`.
Enter the **Input cost per 1K tokens** and the **Output cost per 1K tokens** from your provider's price list.

steps.text: Choose what happens when the money runs out: **Block** or **Warn**.
steps.note: **Block** refuses paid AI calls until next month. **Warn** keeps AI working and notifies AI administrators once.

steps: Select **Save settings**.
sections.result: The card shows **Spent this month** against the budget, with a bar. It also shows the tokens used against your plan's allowance.

sections.title: Privacy and retention
sections.intro: The **Privacy & retention** card protects customer data that goes to an external AI service.

rows: **Redact personal data before calling external providers**
Replaces e-mail addresses, phone numbers, card numbers, and Aadhaar- and PAN-like numbers with placeholders. Card and ID numbers are never put back into answers.
How long each AI call stays in the log, from 7 to 3650 days. The default is 180.

sections.title: Turn AI features on or off
sections.intro: Each AI feature has its own switch. You can also limit a feature to some roles and set how sure the AI must be.
steps: Select the **Features** tab.
In the **Enabled** column, turn each feature on or off.
In **Limit to roles**, add roles to limit who can use the feature. Leave **All roles** to allow everyone.
In **Min. confidence**, enter a number from 0 to 1. The AI acts only when it is at least this sure.
For **Classification**, turn on **Auto-apply** to fill empty fields on new tickets automatically.
Select **Save**.
sections.result: The app shows **AI features saved**.

blocks.caption: The **AI features** table with every feature switched on.
blocks.alt: AI features table with a row per feature showing the Enabled switch, Limit to roles, Min. confidence and Auto-apply

blocks.note: Role limits apply to people who use a feature themselves. AI agents have their own settings. Actions with real consequences always need a person's approval.

sections.title: AI features
sections.intro: These are the features on the **Features** tab.

rows: Suggests the category, product, priority and department of a ticket.
Summarises a conversation, its current status and the pending actions.
Drafts replies from published articles and similar solved tickets, with sources.
Searches by meaning. It suggests articles and similar tickets.
Rates the mood of each customer message and flags frustrated customers.
Finds similar open tickets from the same contact or customer.
Suggests likely causes from similar solved tickets.
Drafts help articles from solved tickets.
Translates text. It needs an external provider.
Estimates the time to solve a ticket from similar tickets.
Checks every hour for unusual ticket volume and notifies supervisors.
Answers report questions written in plain language.
Runs the AI agents. See [Set up AI agents](#ai-agents).
Answers customers in the help center and the chat widget from customer-visible articles.

sections.title: Approve auto-reply scenarios
intro: The auto-responder agent may answer customers on its own, but only inside approved scenarios. A scenario is a type of question, such as how to reset a password.
Without a scenario, the auto-responder never replies by itself. It only proposes replies for an agent to check.
steps: Select the **Auto-reply scenarios** tab.
Select **Add scenario**.
Enter a **Name** and a **Key**, such as `password_reset_howto`.
Enter a **Description** of what the customer asks.
In **Keywords**, add phrases that identify the question, such as `reset password`.
Choose the **Channels** and, if you like, the **Categories (optional)**.
Enter the **Minimum confidence**, from 0.5 to 1.
Optionally add **Approved article ids (optional)**. Replies must then cite one of these articles.
Make sure **Enabled** is on and select **Save scenarios**.
sections.result: The auto-responder can now reply to matching questions on the chosen channels.

blocks.caption: An approved scenario for password reset questions.
blocks.alt: Auto-reply scenario card with Name, Key, Description, Keywords, Channels, Categories, Minimum confidence and Approved article ids

blocks: To stop a scenario, turn off **Enabled**. To remove it, select the bin icon, confirm, and save.

sections.title: Customise a prompt template
intro: A prompt template is the instruction SupportDesk gives the AI for one feature. Each feature has a built-in default.
Change a template only if you need a different tone or extra guidance. Most workspaces keep the defaults.
steps: Select the **Prompt templates** tab.
In the **Templates** list, select a feature.
Edit the **System prompt**, which sets the AI's role and rules.
Edit the **User message template**. Keep the placeholders listed under the field.
To start again, select **Start from default**.
Select **Save as version 1** (or the next number).
sections.result: The app shows that the template was saved as a new version. The list shows the version number instead of **default**.

blocks.caption: The **Classification** prompt with its built-in default active.
blocks.alt: Prompt templates tab with the list of templates, the System prompt and User message template fields, Start from default, Save as version 1 and the Versions card

list: In the **Versions** card, select **Activate** to use another version or the default.
Select **Load** to copy an old version into the editor.
Select **Reset to default** to go back to the built-in prompt. Saved versions are kept.

blocks.note: SupportDesk always adds its security rules to the prompt and checks the AI's answers. A template cannot switch these off.

sections.title: Set up AI agents
intro: AI agents work on tickets when they arrive or when customers reply. They propose actions, such as a category or a reply.
Requests with real consequences always go to a person. Examples are refunds, contracts, and account or data changes.

blocks.caption: The **AI agents** tab with four agents.
blocks.alt: AI agents table with the agent name, kind, mode, scope, runs, Enabled switch, Edit and delete

rows: Classifies new tickets: category, product, department, priority and tags.
Spots missing details, such as the version or the error message. It drafts a request to the customer.
Drafts a solution from published articles and similar solved tickets.
Replies automatically, but only inside approved scenarios, above the threshold and on allowed channels.
Everything becomes a proposal for a person to approve.
The agent fills empty fields and adds tags by itself, above the threshold. The rest is proposed. The auto responder replies inside approved scenarios.

blocks: People with the **Approve, apply and revert AI-proposed actions** permission review proposals. They do this on the **Proposals** tab of the AI Assistant.

blocks.note: Auto-replies are always blocked for critical tickets, frustrated customers and messages that try to trick the AI.

sections.title: Add an AI agent
sections.intro: Start with a triage agent in **Suggest only** mode. Check its proposals for a while before you let it act.
steps: On the **AI agents** tab, select **New agent**.
Enter a **Name** and choose the **Kind**. You cannot change the kind later.
Choose **Suggest only** or **Act on low-risk**.
Optionally choose **Departments** and **Channels**. Empty means all.
Optionally enter a **Minimum confidence**. Empty uses the **Agents** feature setting.
For an auto responder, set **Max automatic replies per ticket** and the **Approved scenarios**. For an info collector, tick the **Information to ask for**.
Under **Allowed actions**, tick the actions the agent may take. None ticked means all.

steps.text: Optionally write **Instructions**, such as the tone to use.
steps.caption: The **New AI agent** dialog for a triage agent.
steps.alt: New AI agent dialog with Name, Kind, the two modes, Departments, Channels, Minimum confidence, Allowed actions and Save agent

steps: Make sure **Enabled** is on and select **Save agent**.
sections.result: The new agent appears in the list. To change it, select **Edit**. To pause it, turn off its switch in the **Enabled** column.

blocks.note: **Instructions** guide external AI services only. The built-in provider uses fixed, reviewed wording.

sections.title: Usage and cost
sections.intro: The **Usage & cost** tab shows how much AI you use and how often people accept its work.

list: Tiles at the top show **Spent this month**, **Monthly budget**, **Budget used**, **Metered tokens (external)** and **AI calls this month**.
Charts show the use **By feature**, **By model** and **By month**.
**Suggestion outcomes** shows, for the last 30 days, how often people accepted, applied, rejected or reverted AI results.
Choose 3, 6 or 12 months in **History**, then select **Refresh**.

blocks.caption: The **Usage & cost** tab with the **Suggestion outcomes** table.
blocks.alt: Usage and cost tab with tiles, charts by feature, model and month, and the Suggestion outcomes table

blocks: **Use rate** is the share of results that people accepted or applied.

sections.title: Check the AI execution log
sections.intro: The execution log lists every AI call. Use it to see what the AI did, what it cost and whether people used the result.

steps.text: Select the **Execution log** tab.
steps.caption: The AI execution log, newest first.
steps.alt: AI execution log with the Feature, Status, Outcome, From and To filters above the list of AI calls

steps: Filter by **Feature**, **Status**, **Outcome**, **From** or **To**.

steps.text: Select a row to open its details.
steps.caption: The details of one AI agent call.
steps.alt: Execution details panel with time, provider, status, outcome, confidence, tokens, cost, latency, prompt version, entity, prompt-injection checks, citations and output

steps: Read the facts, the **Prompt-injection checks** and the **Output**. Select **Ticket · AI view** to open the ticket.
To see more rows, select **Load more** at the bottom of the list.
sections.result: You can see each call's provider, confidence, tokens, cost and result.

rows: The AI answered and the answer passed the checks.
The provider returned an error or an invalid answer.
The call was refused, for example by the plan or a missing permission.
The monthly budget was used up and set to **Block**.
AI or the feature was switched off.

blocks: The outcome shows what people did with the result: **Pending**, **Accepted**, **Applied**, **Rejected**, **Reverted** or **Expired**.

blocks.note: A red shield in the **Injection** column means a message tried to give the AI orders. SupportDesk treated it as data, and agents sent nothing automatically.

sections.title: Where the knowledge settings are
sections.intro: There is no separate knowledge settings page. The settings are in three places.

rows: **Publish, archive and expire articles**, or **Manage knowledge base settings and portals**
Knowledge base, community forums and AI assistant in the help center, and portal languages
The search index used by AI
**Manage AI models, prompts, budgets and agents**
**Manage knowledge base settings and portals**, or a knowledge base role

blocks.caption: **Knowledge Base** > **Categories** with the category tree.
blocks.alt: Knowledge base categories page with Refresh, New category, the filter and the table of categories with visibility, brands, articles and order

sections.title: Organise knowledge base categories
sections.intro: Categories group articles for agents and in the help center. A category's visibility and brands also apply in the portal.
prerequisites: You have the **Publish, archive and expire articles** or **Manage knowledge base settings and portals** permission.
steps: Select **Knowledge Base** > **Categories**.
Select **New category**. To change one, select its pencil icon.
Enter the **Name** and the **Slug**, the short name used in help center addresses.
To nest it, choose a **Parent category**. Leave **Top level** for a main category.
Choose the **Visibility**: **Public**, **Signed-in customers**, **Internal** or **Restricted**.
In **Brands**, choose the brand portals that show it. Empty means every brand portal.
Enter a **Sort order**. Lower numbers come first.
Select **Create category**, or **Save changes** for an existing one.
sections.result: The category appears in the tree. Articles in it follow its visibility in the help center.
blocks: More about articles and categories is in the knowledge base chapter.

sections.title: Rebuild the knowledge index
sections.intro: The knowledge index lets the AI and the search find articles and solved tickets by meaning. It updates itself, but you can rebuild it at once.
steps: Select **Administration** > **AI**.
In the **Embeddings & knowledge index** card, check the **Embedding provider**. **Local (feature hashing, 384 dims)** is free and offline.
If you use an external provider, enter the **Embedding model** and select **Save settings**.
Select **Reindex knowledge now**.
sections.result: The app shows **Knowledge index updated**. The card shows how many articles and solved tickets were indexed.

blocks.note: When you change the embedding model, SupportDesk rebuilds the whole index in the background. Search results may be weaker until it finishes.

chapters.title: Brands and portals
intro: This chapter is for administrators. It explains how to set up a brand and its customer help center, also called the portal.
It also covers logos, footers, the default brand and using your own domain name for the help center.

sections.title: How brands work
intro: A brand is a name your customers know you by. Each brand has its own help center, colours, logo, e-mail footer and sender name.
Channels, knowledge base categories and tickets belong to a brand. Customers see only the help center of their brand.
blocks: To open the list, select **Administration** > **Brands & portals**. You need the **Manage departments, teams, brands and calendars** permission.

blocks.caption: The **Brands & portals** page with one brand.
blocks.alt: Brands and portals page with numbered highlights on New brand, the brand banner, the brand title with its badges, the portal address and the Edit and menu buttons

callouts: **New brand** adds a brand.
The banner in the brand's colours, with its logo or first letter.
The brand name. **Default** marks the main brand. **Portal on** or **Portal off** shows whether the help center is online.
The portal address. Select it to open the help center in a new tab.
**Edit** opens the brand. The menu button has more actions.

blocks.heading: How many brands you can have

blocks: A second brand needs the multi-brand feature of your plan. The Trial plan allows 2 brands, Starter 1, Professional 3 and Enterprise any number.

sections.title: The brand page
sections.intro: Select **Edit** on a brand to open its page. The page has five cards and a live preview of the help center.

blocks.caption: The brand page of the default brand.
blocks.alt: Brand page with numbered highlights on the Identity, Logo and favicon, Custom domain, Portal and Contact and footers cards, the preview and the save bar

callouts: **Identity**: name, portal address and colours.
**Logo & favicon**: the images of the brand.
**Custom domain**: your own address for the help center.
**Portal**: the help center's title, languages, sign-in and features.
**Contact & footers**: support contacts and the footers of the portal and e-mails.
The preview shows the colours, title and welcome message as you type.
The save bar with **Discard** and **Save brand**.

blocks: The save bar shows **Unsaved changes** until you save. **Open portal** at the top right opens the help center.

sections.title: Create a brand
sections.intro: Create a brand for a new company name or product line with its own help center.
prerequisites: You have the **Manage departments, teams, brands and calendars** permission.
Your plan allows another brand.
steps: Select **Administration** > **Brands & portals**, then select **New brand**.

steps.text: Enter the **Brand name**. SupportDesk fills in the **Portal address** from the name.
steps.caption: The **Identity** card of a new brand.
steps.alt: Identity card with Brand name Wings Retail, Portal address wings-retail, Primary colour and Accent colour

steps: Change the **Portal address** if you want a different one. The hint shows the full address.
Choose the **Primary colour** and the **Accent colour**. Use the colour picker or type a code such as `#2563eb`.
In the **Portal** card, enter the **Portal title** and the **Default language**.
Fill in the other cards as needed. See the sections below.
Select **Create brand**.
sections.result: The app shows **Brand created**. You can now upload the logo and favicon.

sections.title: Identity fields
sections.intro: These fields are in the **Identity** card.

rows: The short name in the help center address. Use 2 to 64 lower-case letters, digits and hyphens. It must be unique across SupportDesk.
The main colour of the help center, such as the header. Use a colour code such as `#2563eb`.
The colour of buttons and links. Use a colour code such as `#0ea5e9`.

blocks.note: Some words are reserved and cannot be portal addresses, such as `admin`, `portal` and `widget`.

sections.title: Add a logo and favicon
sections.intro: The logo appears in the help center header and in e-mails. The favicon is the small icon in the browser tab.
prerequisites: The brand is saved. New brands show the upload buttons after you create them.
You have a PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP image of 2 MB or less.
steps: Open the brand.
In the **Logo & favicon** card, select **Upload** next to **Logo**.
Choose the image file. A wide image works best for the logo.
Select **Upload** next to **Favicon** and choose a square image, such as 64 × 64 pixels.
sections.result: The app shows **Logo uploaded** or **Favicon uploaded**. The images appear in the card and in the preview.
blocks: To remove an image, select **Remove** next to it.

blocks.note: SupportDesk checks every uploaded image for malware before it uses it.

sections.title: Set up the help center
sections.intro: The **Portal** card decides what customers see and can do in the brand's help center.
steps: Open the brand and find the **Portal** card.
Enter the **Portal title** and an optional **Welcome message**.
In **Default department for portal tickets**, choose a department. Or keep **Routing decides**.
Enter the **Default language**, such as `en`, and add other codes in **Languages offered**.
Choose how customers sign in, in **Customer sign-in**.
Turn on **Help center is online**.
Turn on the features you want customers to use.
Select **Save brand**.
sections.result: The app shows **Brand saved**. Changes, including the colours, apply in the help center at once.

blocks.caption: The **Portal** card with the help center online.
blocks.alt: Portal card with Portal title, Default department for portal tickets, Welcome message, Default language, Languages offered, Customer sign-in and the feature switches

blocks.note: The feature switches are greyed out while **Help center is online** is off. The default brand's help center cannot be switched off.

sections.title: Help center options
sections.intro: These switches and lists are in the **Portal** card.

rows: Lets customers ask and answer questions.
Lets customers chat with agents from the help center.
Answers from the knowledge base before a customer raises a ticket.
Lets visitors raise tickets without signing in. It needs the help center to be online.
Lets customers create their own help center account.
**E-mail and password / one-time code**, **Single sign-on only** or **Both**.
Where tickets from the help center go. **Routing decides** uses your routing rules.
Up to 20 language codes, such as `en`, `fr` or `pt-BR`.

blocks.note: Customer single sign-on is not available yet. With **Single sign-on only**, the help center hides the password option, and customers sign in with e-mail codes.

sections.title: Set contact details and footers
sections.intro: Add your support contacts and the footers that appear in the help center and in e-mails for this brand.
steps: Open the brand and find the **Contact & footers** card.
Enter the **Support e-mail** and the **Support phone**.

steps.text: Enter the **Portal footer (HTML)**.
steps.note: The help center keeps links, formatting and images in the footer. It removes any other code.

steps: Enter the **E-mail footer / signature (HTML)**.
Check the **E-mail footer preview** below the fields.
Select **Save brand**.
sections.result: The e-mail footer is added to replies, acknowledgements and surveys sent for this brand.

blocks.caption: The **Contact & footers** card with the e-mail footer preview.
blocks.alt: Contact and footers card with Support e-mail, Support phone, Portal footer, E-mail footer and its preview

blocks.tip: Ask someone who knows HTML to write the footers. Plain text also works.

sections.title: Use your own domain for the help center
sections.intro: A custom domain shows the help center under your own address, such as `support.example.com`.
prerequisites: Someone in your company can change your domain's DNS settings, the address book of your web addresses.
steps: Open the brand and find the **Custom domain** card.

steps.text: In **Domain**, enter the address without `https://`, such as `support.example.com`.
steps.caption: The **Custom domain** card with a domain typed in but not yet saved.
steps.alt: Custom domain card with the Domain field filled in

steps: Select **Save brand**. The card now shows the **DNS record to create**.
Give the **Type**, **Name** and **Points to** values to your IT team. They create the record.
After they finish, select **Check DNS**.
sections.result: The badge shows **Connected** when the domain points to SupportDesk. **Points elsewhere** or **Not found** means the record is wrong or not active yet.

blocks.warning: In this release, the help center does not yet open on custom domains. Keep sharing the standard portal address. E-mail links for a brand with a custom domain use that domain, so they do not work yet.

blocks.note: **Check DNS** only compares addresses. It does not prove that you own the domain. Your IT team must also set up a security certificate for the domain.

sections.title: Open a help center or change the default brand
sections.intro: The default brand is your main brand. New channels use it unless you choose another brand.
steps: Select **Administration** > **Brands & portals**.

steps.text: Select the menu button on the brand's card.
steps.caption: The brand menu.
steps.alt: Menu with Open the portal, Make default brand and Delete

steps: Choose **Open the portal** to see the help center in a new tab.
Choose **Make default brand** to make this brand the main brand.
sections.result: The app shows **Default brand changed**. The **Default** badge moves to this brand.

blocks.note: **Make default brand** is greyed out while the brand's help center is offline. Turn on **Help center is online** first.

sections.title: Take a help center offline or delete a brand
sections.intro: Switch a help center off when you stop using a brand. Delete a brand only if it has no tickets and no channels.
steps: To take the help center offline, open the brand, turn off **Help center is online** and select **Save brand**.
To delete a brand, select **Delete** in its menu on the **Brands & portals** page.
In the confirmation, type the brand's portal address to confirm.
Select **Delete**.
sections.result: The app shows **Brand deleted**, and its help center stops working.

blocks.warning: You cannot undo a delete. You cannot delete the default brand, a brand with tickets or a brand with channels. Move its channels to another brand, or switch its help center off instead.

chapters.title: Notification settings and e-mail templates
intro: This chapter is for administrators. It explains how agents are notified by default: in the app, by e-mail, by push or in a digest.
It also shows how to change the wording of the automatic e-mails that SupportDesk sends to customers and agents.

sections.title: The delivery defaults page
intro: To open it, select **Administration** > **Notifications & e-mail templates**. The **Delivery defaults** tab opens first.
You need the **Manage departments, teams, brands and calendars** or the **Manage email accounts and messaging channels** permission.

blocks.caption: The **Delivery defaults** tab with the channel for each event.
blocks.alt: Delivery defaults tab with numbered highlights on the tabs, the information note, the column headings, the first event row, the quiet hours card and the save bar

callouts: The tabs: **Delivery defaults** and **E-mail templates**.
A reminder of how the rules work together.
The four delivery channels. The box in each heading ticks or clears the whole column.
One row per event. Tick the channels that agents get by default.
**Quiet hours & digests**: when e-mail and push wait, and when digests go out.
The save bar with **Discard** and **Save defaults**.

rows: A notification under the bell icon in the desk.
An e-mail right away, or after quiet hours end.
A notification on the mobile app.
The event is bundled into the hourly or daily digest e-mail.

blocks.note: When both **E-mail** and **Digest** are ticked, the event goes into the digest. It does not come as a separate e-mail.

sections.title: Notification events
sections.intro: These are the events on the **Delivery defaults** tab.

rows: A ticket is assigned to the agent.
Someone mentions the agent with @ in a ticket.
A customer replies on a ticket the agent owns or watches.
A ticket the agent is involved in is escalated.
An SLA target is about to be missed.
The agent is asked to approve something.
A request the agent raised was approved or rejected.
The AI proposes an action that needs a decision.
Unusual ticket volume or sentiment is found.
A visitor is waiting in live chat.
A live chat is transferred to the agent or to their department.

sections.title: Set the default channels per event
sections.intro: Decide how agents hear about each event, unless they choose otherwise.
prerequisites: You have the **Manage departments, teams, brands and calendars** or **Manage email accounts and messaging channels** permission.
steps: Select **Administration** > **Notifications & e-mail templates**.
On the **Delivery defaults** tab, tick or clear the boxes for each event.
To change a whole column, tick or clear the box in its heading.
Select **Save defaults**.
sections.result: The app shows **Notification defaults saved**. The save bar shows **All changes saved** and the version number.
blocks: To undo your changes before you save, select **Discard**.

blocks.note: The page says agents can override these defaults. In this release, the desk has no page for agents to do that yet.

sections.title: Set quiet hours and digests
sections.intro: Quiet hours hold back e-mail and push notifications at night. Digests bundle notifications into one e-mail.
steps: On the **Delivery defaults** tab, find the **Quiet hours & digests** card.
Turn on **Quiet hours**.

steps.text: Enter the times in **From** and **Until**, such as `22:00` and `07:00`.
steps.caption: Quiet hours switched on, with the time zone and the digest settings.
steps.alt: Quiet hours and digests card with Quiet hours on, From, Until, Time zone, Digest frequency and Daily digest at

steps: Choose the **Time zone**.
Choose the **Digest frequency**: **Hourly** or **Daily**.
For a daily digest, enter the time in **Daily digest at**. The default is `08:00`.
Select **Save defaults**.
sections.result: E-mail and push notifications wait until quiet hours end. In-app notifications still appear at once.

blocks.note: Critical alerts ignore quiet hours. Quiet hours must end at a different time than they start.

sections.title: E-mail templates
intro: SupportDesk sends four automatic e-mails. Each one has a built-in wording that you can replace with your own.
Select the **E-mail templates** tab to see them.

blocks.caption: The **E-mail templates** tab, grouped by who receives the e-mail.
blocks.alt: E-mail templates tab with numbered highlights on the tabs, the To customers heading, a template name with its badge, its subject line and Edit

callouts: The tabs.
The groups: **To customers** and **To agents**.
The template name and its badge.
The current subject line, and when someone last changed it.
**Edit** opens the template editor.

rows: A customer's e-mail creates a ticket, and the mailbox sends acknowledgements.
A ticket is resolved, and satisfaction surveys are on.
An agent gets an e-mail for a notification, such as an assignment or a mention.
The hourly or daily digest goes out.
You saved your own wording but switched it off, so the built-in wording is used.

sections.title: Customise an e-mail template
sections.intro: Change the subject and text of an automatic e-mail. The preview shows the result with sample values.
steps: On the **E-mail templates** tab, select **Edit** on a template.
Change the **Subject**.
Change the **Body (HTML)**.
To add a value such as the ticket number, place the cursor and select a placeholder chip next to **Insert:**.
Turn on **Use this custom template (off = built-in default)**.
Check the **Preview**. For customer e-mails, choose a brand to see its footer.
Select **Save template**.
sections.result: The app shows **Template saved**. The template's badge changes to **Customised**.

blocks.caption: The editor of the **New ticket acknowledgement** template.
blocks.alt: Template editor with numbered highlights on the title and badges, Subject, Body (HTML), the placeholder chips, the custom template switch, the preview and the save bar

callouts: The template name, who receives it and its badge.
**Subject**: the subject line, up to 500 characters.
**Body (HTML)**: the text of the e-mail.
The placeholder chips. Point to a chip to see what it means.
The switch that turns your wording on or off.
**Preview**: the e-mail with sample values and the brand's footer.
The save bar with **Reset to default**, **Discard** and **Save template**.

blocks.note: SupportDesk removes unsafe code from the e-mail. It inserts values as plain text.

blocks.warning: There is no test send. Check the **Preview** carefully before you save.

sections.title: E-mail template placeholders
sections.intro: A placeholder is a word in double braces. SupportDesk replaces it with the real value when it sends the e-mail. Only the placeholders of each template are allowed.

rows: `{{contact.name}}` customer's name, `{{brand.name}}` brand or mailbox name, `{{ticket.number}}` ticket reference, `{{ticket.subject}}` ticket subject, `{{portal.url}}` help center address.

`{{ticket.number}}`, `{{ticket.subject}}`, `{{agent.name}}` agent who resolved the ticket, `{{survey.link}}` survey address, `{{survey.buttons}}` rating buttons 1 to 5, `{{survey.expires}}` expiry date, `{{brand.name}}`.
`{{user.name}}` agent's name, `{{notification.title}}`, `{{notification.body}}` notification text, `{{notification.link}}` link to the record.
`{{user.name}}`, `{{digest.count}}` number of items, `{{digest.items}}` list of notifications.

blocks.note: If you type a placeholder that the template does not know, the preview warns you. The app does not save the template until you fix it.

sections.title: Go back to the built-in wording
sections.intro: You can switch your wording off for a while, or delete it.
steps: Open the template on the **E-mail templates** tab.
To pause your wording, turn off **Use this custom template (off = built-in default)**. Then select **Save template**.
To delete your wording, select **Reset to default**.
In the confirmation, select **Reset**.
sections.result: The app shows **Template reset to the default**. The badge changes to **Default**.

blocks.warning: **Reset to default** deletes your subject and body. You cannot get them back.

sections.title: How the satisfaction survey e-mail works
sections.intro: The survey e-mail asks the customer to rate the help they got.

list: The rating buttons open the feedback page of the brand's help center, with the chosen star selected.
The customer confirms the rating and can add a comment.
The customer does not need to sign in. The link itself proves who they are, and it expires.
Signed-in customers can also rate a ticket from its page in the help center.

chapters.title: Security, sign-in and API access
intro: This chapter is for administrators. It explains how to protect sign-in to your workspace. That covers multi-factor authentication, password and session rules, the agent IP allow-list and single sign-on.
It also shows how to see and end signed-in sessions. Last, it explains the keys and OAuth clients that other systems use to work with SupportDesk.

sections.title: The Security & sign-in page
intro: Open it with **Administration** > **Security & sign-in**. You need the **Manage password, session, MFA and SSO policies** permission.
The page has three tabs. **Policies** holds the sign-in rules. **Single sign-on** connects your company's sign-in service. **Active sessions** lists who is signed in.

blocks.caption: The **Policies** tab with the default rules of the demo workspace.
blocks.alt: Security and sign-in page with the multi-factor, passwords, sessions and IP allow-list cards

callouts: The tabs: **Policies**, **Single sign-on** and **Active sessions**.
**Multi-factor authentication** sets who must use a second sign-in step.
**Passwords** sets how strong passwords must be, and when an account locks.
**Sessions** sets how long agents stay signed in.
**Agent IP allow-list** limits the networks that agents can work from.
The save bar shows **Unsaved changes**, with **Discard** and **Save policies**.

blocks.note: Your changes apply from the next action each agent takes. If you leave the tab with unsaved changes, the app asks **Discard unsaved changes?** first.

sections.title: Choose who must use multi-factor authentication
sections.intro: Multi-factor authentication adds a second step to sign-in, such as a code from an authenticator app. The sign-in page calls it two-step verification.
prerequisites: You have the **Manage password, session, MFA and SSO policies** permission.
steps: Select **Administration** > **Security & sign-in**.
On the **Policies** tab, under **Multi-factor authentication**, choose an option.
Select **Save policies**.
sections.result: The app shows **Security policies saved**. The rule applies at each person's next sign-in.

rows: Each agent decides whether to use an authenticator app.
People who can manage roles or security cannot switch the second step off. Without an authenticator app, they get a code by e-mail at sign-in.
Every agent signs in with a second step: an authenticator app or a code sent by e-mail.

blocks.note: People who sign in through single sign-on are checked by your identity provider instead.

sections.title: Set the password rules
sections.intro: Password rules apply to new and changed passwords. The lockout rules protect accounts against guessing.
steps: Select **Administration** > **Security & sign-in**.
Under **Passwords**, enter the **Minimum length**.
Enter how many old passwords to block in **Remember previous passwords**.
In **Expire after (days)**, enter how often passwords must change. Enter `0` to keep them until people change them.
Turn on the characters every password needs: **Upper-case letter**, **Lower-case letter**, **Digit** and **Symbol**.
Enter **Lock after failed attempts** and **Lockout duration (minutes)**.
Select **Save policies**.
sections.result: The app shows **Security policies saved**. People with older, weaker passwords meet the new rules when they next change their password.

sections.title: Set how long agents stay signed in
sections.intro: Session rules sign agents out after a quiet period or after a fixed time. The first limit reached wins.
steps: Select **Administration** > **Security & sign-in**.
Under **Sessions**, enter the **Idle timeout (minutes)**.
Enter the **Absolute session lifetime (hours)**.
In **Concurrent sessions per user**, enter how many sign-ins one person can have at once.
If your security team asks for it, change **Access token lifetime (minutes)**.
Select **Save policies**.
sections.result: The app shows **Security policies saved**.

blocks.note: When a person signs in once more than **Concurrent sessions per user** allows, their oldest session ends.

sections.title: Password and session settings
sections.intro: This table lists each setting on the **Policies** tab, with its default and the values you can enter.

rows: Stops people from reusing recent passwords. `0` allows reuse.
Days until a password must change. `0` means never.
Wrong passwords in a row before the account locks.
How long a locked account stays locked.
Characters that every new password must contain.
How long one sign-in token lasts before the app renews it. Short tokens limit the harm of a stolen token.
Signs an agent out after this much inactivity. It cannot be longer than the absolute lifetime.
Signs an agent out after this time, even while they work.
Sign-ins one person can have at the same time.

sections.title: How the agent IP allow-list works
intro: The allow-list limits where agents can work. When it is on, agents can sign in and use SupportDesk only from the listed networks.
The app checks the list at sign-in and at every action. Customers, connected systems and the platform operator are not affected.

list: Enter single addresses, such as `203.0.113.7`, or ranges, such as `10.0.0.0/8`.
Put one entry on each line. You can add up to 100 entries.
The panel on the right shows **Your current address**. **Add my address** adds it to the list.
The app refuses to save a list that does not include your own address. This stops you from locking yourself out.

blocks.note: If every agent seems to come from the same address, your network hides their real addresses. Ask the person who installed SupportDesk to set it up for your network.

sections.title: Restrict agents to your office networks
sections.intro: Use the allow-list when agents must work only from the office or through your company network.
prerequisites: You know the addresses or ranges of your office networks. Your IT team can give them to you.
steps: Select **Administration** > **Security & sign-in**.
Under **Agent IP allow-list**, turn on **Restrict agent access to these networks**.

steps.text: In **Addresses and ranges**, enter one address or range on each line.
steps.caption: The allow-list switched on with one office range. The yellow message warns that your own address is missing.
steps.alt: Agent IP allow-list card with one range entered, the current address and the Add my address button

steps: If the yellow message says your own address is missing, select **Add my address**.

steps.text: Select **Save policies**.
steps.warning: Check the list before you save. Agents outside these networks lose access at their next action.

sections.result: The app shows **Security policies saved**. Agents on other networks see a message that their network is not allowed.

sections.title: Single sign-on
intro: Single sign-on lets agents sign in with their company account. Your identity provider checks who they are. Examples are Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, Google Workspace and Keycloak.
Your plan must include single sign-on to switch it on. Without it, the tab says **Single sign-on is not included in your plan.** You can still prepare the settings.
