A collaborator who can view tickets and add internal notes, but never replies to customers or owns tickets.
An agent's capacity, chat limit, languages, skills and routing attributes, which routing uses to pick an agent.
The team that receives a department's new tickets.
A weekly working pattern in a time zone. Teams can skip agents who are outside their shift.
A product, module, language or other ability that agents hold at a level from 1 to 5.
Working hours and holidays in a time zone. SLA clocks with business hours count only this time.
The order in which SLA policies are checked. The first active policy whose conditions match a ticket wins.
One SLA clock on a ticket: first response, next response or resolution.
A ticket status during which SLA response and resolution clocks stop counting.
A milestone whose target time has passed before the agent met it.
A set of time targets per priority, with conditions and escalation levels, that applies to matching tickets.
A role that an administrator creates or clones. You can change its permissions, data scope and members.
The rule that you cannot grant permissions or a data scope that you do not hold yourself.
One right, such as replying to customers or managing roles. Roles bundle permissions.
A named set of permissions and a data scope that you give to users.
A high-impact permission, such as deleting tickets or managing billing, marked with a Sensitive badge.
One of the six built-in roles. System roles are read-only, but you can clone them.
An extra field that an administrator adds to tickets, contacts or customers.
An arrangement of ticket fields in sections and columns for the agent form or the portal form.
The nature of a request, such as a question, an incident or a change request.
The number of days after resolution during which a customer reply reopens a ticket.
A finer reason within a status, such as Vendor within Waiting on Third Party.
The service that carries a channel's messages, such as Twilio for SMS or Gmail for e-mail.
SupportDesk checking a mailbox for new mail at a set interval.
The web address a provider uses to send new messages to SupportDesk. It is shown in a channel's **Webhook** card.
The code that links the chat widget on your website to a live chat channel.
The mailbox SupportDesk uses for replies on tickets that did not arrive by e-mail.
An administration page that feeds test e-mails, messages and calls into SupportDesk without real providers.
An automatic e-mail that confirms a new ticket to the customer.
An automation that runs actions on a ticket when a trigger fires and the conditions match.
The event that starts a rule, such as a new ticket or a customer reply.
A check on a ticket field that must be true for a rule or transition to apply.
One check of a rule against one event, recorded on the **Executions** tab.
A fixed process of states and transitions that guides a ticket from start to finish.
A step that moves a blueprint ticket from one state to another.
A signed message that SupportDesk sends to another system when an event happens.
A shared secret that the receiving system uses to check that a webhook message came from SupportDesk.
A webhook delivery that failed every retry and is no longer sent automatically.
The AI service that SupportDesk uses, either the built-in one or an external service.
A number pattern that describes the meaning of a text. SupportDesk uses embeddings to search by meaning.
The searchable store of articles and solved tickets that the AI uses to find answers.
A small piece of text that external AI services count to calculate their price.
An approved type of customer question that the auto-responder may answer by itself.
The instruction text that SupportDesk sends to the AI for one feature.
Text in a customer message that tries to give the AI orders. SupportDesk treats it as data only.
The customer portal of a brand, where customers read articles, raise tickets and follow them.
The short name in a help center's web address, such as `wings`.
The main brand of the workspace. Its help center must stay online.
Your own web address for a help center, such as `support.example.com`.
An entry in your domain's settings that tells browsers where an address points.
The small icon that browsers show in the tab of a web page.
The administrator's choice of how agents are notified of each event: in the app, by e-mail, by push or in a digest.
The subject and text of an automatic e-mail that SupportDesk sends.
A second sign-in step after the password, such as a code from an authenticator app or an e-mailed code. The sign-in page calls it two-step verification.
Signing in to SupportDesk with your company account, checked by your identity provider.
The service that checks who your staff are, such as Microsoft Entra ID, Okta or Google Workspace.
The list of network addresses from which agents may use SupportDesk.
A secret that a script or another system uses to work with SupportDesk, limited to chosen scopes.
An id and secret that another system swaps for a one-hour pass to work with SupportDesk.
One area that a key or OAuth client may use, such as reading tickets.
Wings' business software that holds customer masters, installations, licences and AMC contracts. SupportDesk can sync with it.
One run that brings changed records from another system into SupportDesk.
The system where engineers manage bugs and features: Azure DevOps, GitHub or the built-in engineering board.
Rules that decide what linked tickets get when engineering work is resolved or released.
A private address in Teams or Slack that accepts posts for one channel.
A shared password that proves a tracker's messages really come from your tracker.
The tamper-evident record of sensitive actions in your workspace.
The way audit entries are linked, each with a fingerprint of the one before. A broken link shows that an entry was changed or removed.
A rule that archives, anonymises or deletes a kind of data after a number of days.
A count of what a retention policy would affect now, without changing anything.
A rule that preserves matching tickets and their records during a dispute, audit or investigation.
A customer's request to get a copy of their data or to have it erased.
To remove personal text from records but keep the numbers for reports.
Time-limited, read-only diagnostic access that you can grant to SupportDesk staff.
The settings that shape how your desk works, such as statuses, fields, SLA policies, rules and templates.
An imported configuration file that waits for review. Nothing changes until you publish it.
A copy of your complete configuration at one moment, with a version number.
Returning your configuration to an earlier snapshot.
The package you pay for. It sets the price per agent, the limits and the included features.
One paid agent licence.
How often you pay: monthly, or annually with two months free.
The days after a missed payment or an ended trial when the workspace still works normally.
The state after the grace period. People can sign in, read and pay, but cannot change anything.
Charged only for the part of the period that remains.
A new workspace you can use free for at least 14 days, with every feature of the chosen plan.
How many tickets a portal user sees: only their own, their location's, or their whole organisation's.
A portal filter for tickets where support replied to you or asked you to confirm a resolution.
The time after a ticket closes during which the customer can still reopen it. Each ticket shows its last reopen date.
A one-time 6-digit code sent by e-mail. It signs you in without a password and works for 10 minutes.
Help articles the portal shows while you type a ticket or topic, in case one already answers your question.
The reply that the person who asked a community question marked as the one that solved it.
A step-by-step set of questions in the portal that leads to a fix or to a ticket for the support team.
The 1 to 5 star score a customer gives a resolved or closed ticket, with an optional comment.
The mobile app mode for agents. It shows queues, tickets, alerts and approvals.
The mobile app mode for customers. It shows their requests, a new request form and help articles.
The portal name a customer enters in the mobile app, such as `wings`. It is the part of the portal address after `/portal/`.
Replies, notes and new requests that the mobile app holds until it has a connection.
A message written offline in the mobile app. The app sends it when the connection returns.
A message that appears on a phone even when the app is closed. The standard SupportDesk app does not send them yet.
A state of the mobile app while offline. You can read saved screens, but changes wait for a connection.
A customer company that uses SupportDesk. Each tenant has one workspace.
The separate part of SupportDesk where platform operators manage tenants, plans, invoices and support access.
A subscription whose trial ended or whose invoice is overdue. The workspace keeps working until the grace period ends.
A cancelled tenant whose keep-data period has ended. Its data waits to be deleted.
A payment made outside SupportDesk, such as a bank transfer. An operator records it with **Mark paid**.
An invoice that an operator cancelled. Nobody needs to pay it.
The monthly value of all active and past-due subscriptions.
The total amount of all unpaid invoices.
Usage, configuration counts, failed background work and recent audit entries of a tenant. They never include tickets or customer data.
A data store used by one tenant only, instead of the store that tenants share.
